problem_stated.one_line: LLM agents deployed in persistent roles meet a continuous stream of tasks but do not learn from accumulated interaction history; existing agent memory stores raw trajectories or success-only workflows, which are neither transferable nor able to exploit failures.

verbatim_quotes.quote: As these agents are increasingly deployed in persistent, long-running roles, they naturally encounter a continuous stream of tasks and interactions. However, a critical limitation persists: they largely fail to learn from this accumulated experience. By approaching each new task in isolation, they are doomed to (i) repeat similar errors observed in the past, (ii) discard valuable insights gained from related problems, and, most importantly, (iii) lack self-evolving capabilities that make the agent system more capable over time.

They suffer from two fundamental drawbacks. First, they lack the ability to distill higher-level, transferable reasoning patterns. Second, by over-emphasizing successful experiences, they leave the valuable lessons from an agent's own failures largely underexplored (Zhang et al., 2024). Consequently, existing memory designs often remain limited to passive record-keeping rather than providing actionable, generalizable guidance for future decisions.

This streaming setting highlights two key challenges: (i) how to extract and preserve useful memory from past trajectories, and (ii) how to effectively leverage such memory for future queries to avoid redundantly re-discovering already successful strategies or repeating past mistakes.
no ground truth is available during test-time, so the agent must continually evolve by only leveraging its own past trajectories and any self-verification without relying on external labels.

how_it_differs_from_canonical_U_E: Canonical (U-E) summarises the *context* $c_k$ of a future query before that query arrives. ReasoningBank summarises the agent's own *trajectory* from a past query. The object written is experience, not context — this is exactly what makes it the closest E-path analogue of consolidation.
$S(\cdot; B_s)$ is gated by a self-produced binary label $j_k$; the canonical form has no such gate. The failure branch $S_{-}$ has no counterpart in the canonical write at all.
$\mathrm{wr}$ is pure union. There is no compaction operator, so the rate-distortion question that $C_{\text{cap}}$ exists to ask is never posed.

In MaTTS, $B_s$ is spent generating *new experience* ($m$ rollouts) rather than on processing existing experience — a budget mode the canonical (U-E) does not contemplate. The rollouts are simultaneously wake-time compute for the current task and sleep-time material for the next.

outer_vs_inner.prose: For the reader who has never trained a model: an outer loop (gradient descent on $\Theta$) does not occur in this paper at any point. What the paper calls 'learning', 'self-evolving' and 'test-time learning' is entirely the growth of a text file. The only thing that changes between task 1 and task 187 is the contents of $E$ and hence the system prompt. This is the defining property of the E-path and it is why the paper can claim continual improvement without any of the machinery (replay buffers, EWC, LoRA merging, checkpoint management) that the $\Theta$-path requires.

update_layer.which: (U-E) only. $\Theta$ is frozen and $W$ does not exist in this system.
update_layer.order: Single layer, so no ordering question arises across layers. Within the round the order is: $\mathrm{ret}(E_k,q_k)$ (read) → wake-time rollout → $j_k$ (self-judge) → $S(\cdot;B_s,j_k)$ (extract) → $\mathrm{wr}$ (append). One round per task.
differences_from_canonical_U_E: Argument of $S$: the canonical $\hat c_k = S(c_k;B_s)$ processes a *context*; here $S$ processes the agent's own trajectory, i.e. $\hat c_k = S(\mathcal{H}^{\Delta}_k; B_s, j_k)$. Experience, not context.
Label gate: $S$ branches on a self-produced binary $j_k$, with a distinct prompt per branch. The failure branch is the paper's headline novelty and has no analogue in the canonical form.

Write operator: $\mathrm{wr}(E_k,\hat c_k) = E_k \cup \hat c_k$, a pure union. No merge, no eviction, no decay. The paper states this is deliberate to isolate the contribution of content quality [App A.2 txt:1932-1936; App E 'Simplicity in memory retrieval and consolidation' txt:2461-2465].

Cardinality bound: $|\hat c_k| \le 3$ (single trajectory) or $\le 5$ (MaTTS parallel over $m$ trajectories) — the only capacity control in the entire system, and it bounds the write rate, not the pool size.

MaTTS variant: $B_s$ is partly spent *manufacturing* the experience to be summarised ($m$ rollouts), not only on summarising it. Written in the unified frame: $\mathcal{H}^{\Delta}_k = \mathrm{gen}(q_k, \mathrm{ret}(E_k,q_k); B_s^{\text{roll}})$ followed by $\hat c_k = S(\mathcal{H}^{\Delta}_k; B_s^{\text{sum}})$. This borrows the $\mathrm{gen}(\cdot;B_s)$ idea from (U-$\Theta$) but feeds the result to (U-E) instead of to a gradient step.
update_layer.the_theta_path_it_does_not_take: The structure $\mathcal{R}_k = \mathrm{gen}(\mathcal{H}_k;B_s)$ followed by a $\Theta$ update is exactly what ReasoningBank stops one step short of: it builds $\mathcal{R}_k$ (a self-generated, self-labelled, success/failure-partitioned corpus of distilled strategies) and then, instead of running $\eta_\Theta \nabla_\Theta \mathcal{L}$, it prepends the corpus to the prompt. Naming this is the chapter's main bridge-out to the $\Theta$-path.

Since a WebArena trajectory averages ~8 steps and the whole task costs ~50k tokens, the raw-trajectory part of the store dominates the distilled part by roughly three orders of magnitude. The paper never notes this and never measures it.

rho.detail: No forgetting rate, no per-round degradation measurement, no interference metric, no re-evaluation of earlier tasks after the pool has grown. The word 'forgetting' appears once, only as future work: 'more advanced consolidation mechanisms (e.g., merging, forgetting) can be incorporated in future work' [App A.2, txt:1935-1936].
rho.nearest_related_evidence: §C.1 measures degradation with respect to the number of RETRIEVED experiences, not with respect to pool age: SR = 39.0 (0 experiences), 49.7 (1), 46.0 (2), 45.5 (3), 44.4 (4) on WebArena-Shopping / Gemini-2.5-flash [Figure 13, txt:2077-2111]. The paper's reading: 'while memory provides valuable guidance, excessive experiences may introduce conflicts or noise.' This is retrieval interference at a fixed pool, and must NOT be reported as $\rho$.
rho.why_this_matters: $\rho$ is the quantity that decides whether repeated sleep rounds are sustainable. With an append-only store and a monotone degradation curve in the number of injected experiences, the paper has assembled exactly the ingredients for measuring $\rho$ and does not measure it.

amortisation_equation_A.why: Equation (A) needs $N_q$, the number of queries that share one context. In ReasoningBank each task is its own context ($N_q=1$); the reuse is across tasks, mediated by a top-1 cosine retrieval. The paper never reports how often any stored item is retrieved, nor the hit-rate distribution, nor how many future tasks benefit from a given item. Without a retrieval-count distribution the break-even $N_q^*$ is undefined.
amortisation_equation_A.what_can_be_computed_instead: A per-task overhead ratio: sleep cost / wake cost = 3748.4 / 49306.1 = 7.60% (my arithmetic on Table 5), against a +20.5% relative SR gain on WebArena overall with Gemini-2.5-flash [§C.2, txt:2163-2166]. This is a one-round accounting, not an amortisation over $N_q$.

new.concept: reasoning memory / memory item = {title, description, content}
new.definition: A strategy-level, environment-agnostic text unit distilled from one trajectory, deliberately stripped of site names, queries and literal strings by prompt instruction.
new.why_new: It is a third point on the E-path content spectrum, after raw trajectory (Synapse) and procedural workflow (AWM). The paper's whole empirical case is that content form, not memory architecture, is the binding constraint. [§3.2 Memory Schema, txt:327-332; App E 'Focus on memory content', txt:2456-2460]

new.definition: A memory item produced by a distinct extraction prompt that first reflects on why a trajectory failed and then states a preventative strategy.
new.why_new: It makes the write operation in (U-E) label-conditional. Prior E-path work writes only what worked. [§3.2, txt:344-346; App A.1 Fig. 9 right panel]

new.concept: self-judged write gate (LLM-as-a-Judge as signal provider)
new.definition: A binary success/failure label produced by the same frozen backbone with no ground truth, used solely to route the extraction prompt.
new.why_new: It is the E-path's substitute for the verification step that the Theta-path needs before writing to weights, and it is far cheaper (2186.3 tokens/task) than any verifier the Theta-path could afford. [§3.2, txt:341-346; Table 5]

new.definition: Spending wake-time budget on m rollouts (parallel) or m self-refinements (sequential) for the SAME query, then harvesting the contrast between them into E via a single aggregation prompt.
new.why_new: It couples B_t and B_s: the same tokens serve the current answer and the next round's write. No other paper in the corpus does this. [§3.3, txt:353-464]

new.concept: memory-driven experience scaling as a scaling dimension
new.definition: The claim that quality improves along an axis of accumulated, distilled experience, distinct from parameters, data, and test-time compute.
new.why_new: This is the paper's framing contribution and the E-path's answer to the A3 spine candidate in S0 §6. Note it is asserted, not fitted — the paper reports no exponent, no saturation point, and no functional form. [abstract txt:24-25; §1 txt:166-167]

new.definition: 'Instead of scaling experience through breadth by adding more tasks, we focus on scaling experience through depth by tackling each single task with more exploration.' [§1, txt:160-162]
new.why_new: A clean vocabulary for splitting the B_s budget: more rounds vs richer rounds.

bridge_out_for_the_monograph: 'decay/refresh policies' (App D) is the paper's own name for $\rho$, and it is listed as future work. This is the exact handoff to the Theta-path chapters on algorithmic forgetting (SCM) and to the rate-distortion capacity chapter: the E-path arrives at the same question from the opposite direction and does not answer it.

The paper builds $\mathcal{R}_k$ — a self-generated, self-labelled, success/failure-partitioned corpus — and then declines to run $\eta_\Theta \nabla_\Theta \mathcal{L}$ on it. SEAL's self-edit and the Theta-path 'dreaming' chapters take precisely that next step. This is the sharpest available bridge between E-4 and the Theta-path, and it must be made by this book because the paper does not make it.

The MaTTS finding that extra rollouts only pay off when memory is good ('scaling alone is insufficient', §4.4) is a constraint any Theta-path synthetic-data pipeline inherits: the quality of $\mathrm{gen}(\mathcal{H}_k;B_s)$ is bounded by the quality of what the generator already knows.

unfavorable_facts.fact: Consolidation is a bare append. There is no merging, pruning, deduplication, eviction, decay, or overwrite anywhere in the system, and the store keeps the full raw trajectory alongside the distilled items. So the 'consolidation' in the paper's closed loop is not consolidation in the sense the rest of this corpus uses the word, and the store grows without bound.
unfavorable_facts.location: §3.2 txt:347-349; App A.2 'Memory Consolidation' txt:1932-1936; 'ReasoningBank Storage' txt:1937-1942

unfavorable_facts.fact: More memory monotonically hurts. Injecting 1 retrieved experience gives 49.7 SR; 2 gives 46.0; 3 gives 45.5; 4 gives 44.4. The default configuration is therefore the minimum non-zero setting, and the reported gains are gains from ONE retrieved experience (at most 3 items). The paper does not test whether the same degradation appears with a larger pool at fixed retrieval count.
unfavorable_facts.severity: high — it bounds the method's headroom and contradicts the 'scaling dimension' framing

unfavorable_facts.fact: The §4.4 prose contradicts its own numbers. The paper writes 'scaling actually reduces performance for weaker memories, where Synapse slightly increases from 40.6 to 41.2, and AWM from 44.4 to 45.5.' Both quoted numbers are increases, not reductions.
unfavorable_facts.severity: medium — the asymmetry claim ('This asymmetry highlights that scaling alone is insufficient') rests on a difference in magnitude (+0.6, +1.1 vs +3.3), not on a sign flip as stated

unfavorable_facts.fact: Table 4's relative-reduction figure does not check out. The paper claims 'up to 2.1 fewer steps (a 26.9% relative reduction)'. 2.1/6.8 = 30.9%. No pair of cells in Table 4 produces 26.9%.
unfavorable_facts.severity: low individually, but it is an arithmetic error in the paper's own headline efficiency claim

unfavorable_facts.fact: The Multi subset, which carries the paper's generalization claim ('+4.6 averaged SR over the strongest baseline'), has only 29 instances. One task is worth 3.4 points. On Claude-3.7-Sonnet the entire column reads No Memory 0.0, Synapse 0.0, AWM 0.0, ReasoningBank 3.4, +MaTTS 10.3 — i.e. 0, 0, 0, 1 and 3 solved tasks.

unfavorable_facts.severity: high — the most-cited generalization result is a 29-instance result

unfavorable_facts.fact: The LLM-as-a-Judge that gates every write is only 72.7% accurate against ground truth, and the robustness study does not use real judges. Different accuracy levels are SIMULATED by flipping ground-truth labels with a given probability, which produces independent symmetric noise. Real judge error is neither independent nor symmetric — a judge tends to fail systematically on a class of ambiguous tasks, and those are exactly the tasks whose memory items matter.
unfavorable_facts.severity: high — this is the paper's only defence of its central unverified signal

unfavorable_facts.fact: The same robustness study consumes ground-truth labels to build its simulated verifiers, including a 100% setting that 'uses the ground-truth labels directly' — inside a method whose stated premise is that no ground truth is available at test time. The 100% point is therefore an oracle, not an achievable configuration.
unfavorable_facts.location: §5 txt:1300-1313 against the setup in §3.1 txt:307-309
unfavorable_facts.severity: medium

The 'cost-effectiveness' conclusion of §C.2 does not cover any MaTTS number in Table 1.

unfavorable_facts.severity: high — this is exactly the cell the monograph needs and it is missing

unfavorable_facts.severity: medium

unfavorable_facts.severity: medium — it establishes that E-path writes carry a real downside risk

unfavorable_facts.fact: No claim is ever verified about the memory actually being used. Retrieval matches on the embedding of the task QUERY, not on item content; the injected instruction leaves usage to the model's discretion ('You can use it when you feel it's relevant'); and no retrieval hit-rate, item-reuse count, or attribution analysis is reported. The causal chain from a stored item to a behaviour change is supported only by hand-picked case studies (Figures 6, 15, 16, 17).
unfavorable_facts.severity: high — it is what prevents computing $N_q$ and hence equation (A)

unfavorable_facts.fact: The emergent-behaviour result — the paper's most quoted qualitative claim, that memory items evolve from procedural rules to compositional strategies — is one hand-selected memory item, presented as 'a human case study', with no quantification, no counts, and no control.
unfavorable_facts.severity: medium

unfavorable_facts.fact: The agent's observations are not the environment observations. 'We use the thinking process of pi_L as the approximation of o_{0:t} due to lengthy observation representations', following AWM. So what is judged, distilled and stored is the model's own narration of what it saw, not what it saw.
unfavorable_facts.severity: medium — self-narration in, self-narration out; error modes where the model misreads the page are invisible to both the judge and the extractor

unfavorable_facts.fact: The WebArena Map domain is excluded, so 'WebArena' here is a 684-instance subset of the benchmark, not the full benchmark.
unfavorable_facts.severity: low

unfavorable_facts.fact: The store is per independent run and has no user, session, or tenant model, no privacy discussion, and no contamination discussion — even though the items are free text distilled by an LLM from trajectories that in a real deployment would contain user data. The judge and extractor also run on the same backbone as the agent, so a systematically biased backbone biases the labels, the items, and the actions in a single closed loop with no external check.
unfavorable_facts.severity: medium

unfavorable_facts.fact: The efficiency comparison is not compute-matched. ReasoningBank pays an extra judge call and an extra extraction call per task that No Memory does not pay; the paper's step-count and token comparisons against No Memory are therefore comparisons at different total budgets. The paper does report the 4.3% total-token gap, but the SR comparison in Table 1 is never budget-normalised.
unfavorable_facts.severity: medium

unfavorable_facts.fact: The paper reports no absolute storage or latency quantity of any kind — no bytes, no ms, no dollars, no throughput — while §C.2 is explicitly framed as being 'to facilitate real-world deployment'.

unfavorable_facts.severity: high for this monograph specifically — three of the four cost cells are empty

cross_path_citations.summary: ReasoningBank engages ONLY the E-path, and only its agent-memory wing. It cites nothing from the W-path and nothing from the Theta-path. Within the E-path it does not cite the paper that named this line.

cited: MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023, arXiv 2310.08560) — one citation, as an example of plain-text memory storage. §2, txt:188-189. No engagement with its OS/paging argument.
Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025, arXiv 2504.19413) — one citation, grouped under 'structured graphs' with MemOS (Li et al. 2025b) and A-Mem (Xu et al. 2025). §2, txt:189-190.
Synapse (Zheng et al., 2024, ICLR 2024) — baseline, trajectory memory.

AWM / Agent Workflow Memory (Wang et al., 2025d, ICML 2025) — baseline, workflow memory; also the source of the observation-approximation trick (footnote 1) and of the LLM-classifier protocol (App A.2 txt:1865).

ExpeL (Zhao et al., 2024), Dynamic Cheatsheet (Suzgun et al., 2025), AgentKB (Tang et al., 2025b), Memp (Fang et al., 2025), MemoryBank (Zhong et al., 2024), Reflective Memory Management (Tan et al., 2025), Contextual Experience Replay (Liu et al., 2025b) — the agent-memory neighbourhood.
NOT_cited: Sleep-time Compute (Letta, arXiv 2504.13171) — ABSENT. The phrase 'sleep-time compute' does not occur; the string 'sleep' does not occur anywhere in the paper (verified by grep over all 2481 lines).

W_path.detail: No Titans, no test-time training, no fast weights, no linear-attention state, no RNN/SSM memory. The strings 'fast weight', 'test-time training', 'Titans' do not occur. The two nearest citations are memoryLLM/M+ (Wang et al., 2025b, ICML 2025), cited once as 'latent embeddings' among memory FORMS (§2 txt:189) and once as 'long-term consolidated knowledge' in future work (App D txt:2417), and EM-LLM (Fountas et al., 2025, ICLR 2025), cited once in App D as 'episodic traces'. Neither is engaged as an update rule; both appear as items in a taxonomy of storage forms.
W_path.note: The paper's own phrase 'test-time learning' (§3.1, txt:305-307) is cited to Wang et al. 2025c ('Inducing programmatic skills for agentic tasks') and Wu et al. 2024a (StreamBench) — i.e. to the streaming-agent literature, not to the TTT literature. Same words, disjoint reference sets.

Theta_path.detail: No LoRA, no PEFT, no model editing (ROME/MEMIT), no SEAL, no EWC, no generative replay, no distillation into weights, no catastrophic forgetting. cross_path_citations.what_the_monograph_should_report: This is the corpus's clearest instance of the S0 §5 'silence between paths' finding, and it runs in three directions at once. (1) The E-path's most-cited 2025-26 agent-memory paper does not cite the paper that gave sleep-time compute its name, even though both write summaries of past context to an external store before the next query. (2) It shares no vocabulary with the W-path despite both claiming 'test-time learning'. (3) It builds the exact training corpus that the Theta-path consumes and never mentions that the Theta-path exists. The three communities in this monograph are, as of this paper, not in contact.

systems_implications.claim: The wake path gets CHEAPER, not more expensive, despite injecting memory into the system prompt.
systems_implications.grounding: PAPER NUMBER. Action-generation tokens fall from 50847.4 (No Memory) to 49306.1 (ReasoningBank), -3.03%, and WebArena overall steps fall 9.7 -> 8.3 (flash), 8.8 -> 7.4 (pro), 8.0 -> 7.3 (claude). [Table 5 §C.2; Table 1]
systems_implications.why: In a ReAct loop the context is re-sent and re-prefilled every step, and it grows with the trajectory. Removing one step removes not just one decode but one full prefill of an already-long context. Injecting ~3 short items into the system prompt costs a fixed handful of tokens per step; removing 1.4 steps saves a whole step's worth of accumulated context. [INFERENCE from the ReAct definition in App B.1 txt:2036-2038, grounded in the two numbers above.]

systems_implications.claim: The entire net serving overhead of this method is 3748.4 tokens per task, of which 58% is the judge and 42% is the extractor.
systems_implications.grounding: PAPER NUMBER. Table 5: judge 2186.3 + extraction 1562.1 = 3748.4; total overhead vs No Memory = +4.3%. [§C.2 txt:2153-2192]
systems_implications.why: Both are single-shot, offline, batchable calls with no interactivity requirement and no latency SLA. In a real deployment they are the ideal filler workload for idle accelerators: known input length, no user waiting, fully parallel across tasks. This is the E-path's structural advantage over the Theta-path, where the equivalent step is a training job with optimizer state and a checkpoint write.

systems_implications.claim: Nothing per-user lands in weights, so shared-weight batching survives intact.
systems_implications.grounding: PAPER FACT that $\Theta$ is never updated (§4.1, App B.1: models are consumed through the Vertex AI API). [INFERENCE] Therefore all users share one weight copy; the per-user state is a JSON blob plus an embedding vector, and the only per-request divergence is prompt content.
systems_implications.why: This is the decisive serving contrast with the Theta-path, where a per-user delta breaks weight sharing across a batch. It is the Rosetta row 'batch로 weight 공유 / Θ-경로에서 깨짐' seen from the E side.

systems_implications.claim: Prefix caching is degraded, not helped, by the memory injection.
systems_implications.grounding: [INFERENCE, not in the paper.] Retrieved items are concatenated into the SYSTEM instruction [App A.2 txt:1869-1874], i.e. at the very front of the prompt. Because the retrieved set differs per task, the shared system prefix that would otherwise be identical across all tasks is broken at position ~0, so a served fleet loses cross-task prefix-cache reuse of the system block. Placing memory after the static system block would preserve it. The paper does not discuss prompt layout or caching at all.
systems_implications.why: Worth stating explicitly in the chapter because it is a real, avoidable serving cost that the token accounting in Table 5 does not capture (Table 5 counts tokens, not cache hits).

systems_implications.claim: Retrieval is a linear scan over a growing JSON store with precomputed embeddings — host-side, not accelerator-side.
systems_implications.grounding: PAPER FACT: 'Similarity search is conducted over the memory pool using cosine distance'; embeddings 'pre-computed for each given query and stored in another JSON file' [App A.2 txt:1869-1872, 1937-1942]. No index structure is mentioned. [INFERENCE] Cost is one embedding API call plus an O(n) dot-product sweep, n = number of stored experiences; at n in the hundreds this is microseconds of CPU and is invisible next to a 50k-token LLM task.
systems_implications.why: The state lives in host DRAM / disk, not in HBM. Unlike the W-path, where the fast-weight state must be resident and moved with the model, the E-path's state touches the accelerator only as prompt tokens. This is why E-path capacity is cheap and E-path READ bandwidth is expensive (every retrieved byte becomes a prefilled token).

systems_implications.claim: The read cost of E is paid in prefill tokens on every step, not once per session.
systems_implications.grounding: [INFERENCE from App A.2 txt:1869-1874 (items concatenated into the system instruction) and App B.1 txt:2036-2038 (a step is a full observe-think-act LLM call).] In a ReAct loop the system prompt is re-submitted every step, so an item of $b$ tokens costs $b \times$ (number of steps) prefill tokens per task, i.e. ~8x on WebArena. The paper never separates prompt from completion tokens, so this cannot be quantified from Table 5.
systems_implications.why: It is the E-path's real bandwidth story and it changes the design conclusion: item BREVITY matters more than item count. It also explains §C.1's degradation curve as a cost as well as a quality effect.

systems_implications.claim: The store keeps full raw trajectories, so the bytes are dominated by material that is never read.
systems_implications.grounding: PAPER FACT: 'each entry of ReasoningBank consists of a task query, the original trajectory, and the corresponding memory items' [App A.2 txt:1937-1939], while retrieval injects only titles and contents [txt:1872-1874]. [INFERENCE] The distilled part is at most 3 items of 1-3 sentences (order 100 tokens); the raw trajectory is order 10k tokens. So >98% of the store is cold. A deployment could tier the raw trajectories to cold storage with no behavioural change.
systems_implications.why: It is a concrete, checkable systems consequence that the paper leaves on the table, and it is the E-path's version of the capacity question.

systems_implications.claim: MaTTS is a throughput problem, not a latency problem, and it is the one configuration that would hurt a real deployment.
systems_implications.grounding: PAPER FACT: k=5 parallel rollouts per task plus a self-contrast call plus a Best-of-N selector call over all 5 trajectories [Table 1 caption; App A.3 txt:1943-1990]. [INFERENCE] Wake compute is ~5x, and the BoN selector's prompt contains all five full trajectories, so its prefill is ~5x a single trajectory — the single largest prompt in the system. Under a fixed-QPS serving budget this is a 5x capacity cost bought for +2.1 to +3.3 SR points (e.g. flash Shopping 49.7 -> 53.0 pass@1).
systems_implications.why: The chapter's judgement material for Part III: on this evidence, MaTTS is an offline-quality knob, not a serving configuration.

systems_implications.claim: Step reduction is the metric that would actually show up in a production dashboard, and it is where the method's gain is largest in relative terms.
systems_implications.grounding: PAPER NUMBERS. Table 4: on successful WebArena-Shopping instances, 6.8 -> 4.7 steps. Figure 16 case study: 29 -> 10 steps. SWE-Bench-Verified: 30.3 -> 27.5 (flash), 21.1 -> 19.8 (pro).
systems_implications.why: Each removed step is one full LLM round trip plus one environment round trip. For an agent product the step count, not the token count, sets both wall-clock and the number of chances to break something. The paper never converts steps into seconds, so $L_w$ stays absent.

systems_implications.claim: The write path has no durability, concurrency, or consistency story.
systems_implications.grounding: PAPER FACT: 'We persist the memory pool for each independent run' into JSON files [App A.2 txt:1937-1942]. [INFERENCE] A single-writer JSON file cannot support concurrent agents sharing a bank, which is exactly the deployment the paper's future-work section proposes ('a deployable memory service that scales across domains and teams', App D txt:2422-2424). Append-only union semantics happen to be conflict-free, which is the one thing that would make sharding easy.
systems_implications.why: Names the gap between the artifact evaluated and the service proposed.
